concepts.title: Choosing the right chart
concepts.kw: chart choice line chart bar chart scatter plot histogram pie chart stacked bar visualisation best practices axis colour
concepts.s: The right chart depends on the question: change over time, comparing categories, showing a distribution, or showing a relationship.
concepts.d: Use a line chart for trends over time, a bar chart to compare categories (sorted, horizontal when labels are long), a histogram or box plot for distributions, and a scatter plot for the relationship between two numeric variables. Pie charts only work for a few parts of one whole; bars are usually clearer. Stacked bars make only the bottom segment easy to compare. Start bar axes at zero, label directly instead of relying on legends, use colour to highlight the point rather than decorate, and put the main message in the title.
concepts.e: To show that Android conversion fell after a release, use a line chart of daily conversion by platform with the release date marked and the title "Android checkout conversion fell 9 points after v6.2".
concepts.c: Why must a bar chart's axis start at zero, while a line chart's doesn't have to?
concepts.i: Interviewers show a poor chart and ask how you'd improve it, or ask which chart you'd use for a given question.

concepts.title: Data storytelling and executive summaries
concepts.kw: data storytelling executive summary narrative insight recommendation so what audience stakeholders presentation pyramid principle
concepts.s: Data storytelling turns analysis into a clear message that a busy audience can act on: what happened, why it matters, and what to do.
concepts.d: Lead with the answer, following the pyramid principle: the main finding and recommendation first, then the supporting evidence. Know the audience and what decision they face; executives want the impact and the ask, while specialists want the method. Each slide or chart makes one point, stated in its title. Quantify impact in business terms, such as revenue or customers affected, and state your confidence and caveats honestly. End with clear next steps and owners. Keep the details in an appendix for those who want them.
concepts.e: "Repeat purchases fell 8 points for April's cohort because of late first deliveries in Hyderabad. Fixing courier allocation there could recover about Rs 40 lakh a quarter. We recommend reallocating two courier partners by June."
concepts.c: Why should an executive summary start with the recommendation rather than the method?
concepts.i: Expect to present a finding to a non-technical stakeholder, or to summarise an analysis in a few sentences.

concepts.title: Power BI essentials: data model and DAX
concepts.kw: power bi dax measures calculated columns data model star schema relationships power query filter context row context calculate time intelligence
concepts.s: Power BI is Microsoft's BI tool. Good reports depend on a clean data model, Power Query for preparation, and DAX measures for calculations.
concepts.d: Power Query shapes the data before loading. The model should be a star schema: fact tables related to dimension tables, with single-direction relationships and a proper date table for time intelligence. DAX measures calculate at query time in the current filter context, while calculated columns are computed row by row at refresh and stored. CALCULATE changes the filter context, which is the core of most DAX, for example sales for the same period last year. Import mode is fast; DirectQuery queries the source live. Row-level security restricts what each user sees.
concepts.e: A measure Sales LY = CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date])) works for any slicer selection because it modifies the filter context, which a calculated column can't do.
concepts.c: Why should total sales be a measure rather than a calculated column?
concepts.i: Expect questions on star schemas in Power BI, measures versus calculated columns, filter context, CALCULATE, and import versus DirectQuery.

concepts.title: Tableau essentials
concepts.kw: tableau dimensions measures calculated fields lod expressions fixed include exclude extracts live connection dashboards parameters filters order of operations
concepts.s: Tableau is a visual analytics tool where you build charts by dragging dimensions and measures onto shelves, then combine them into interactive dashboards.
concepts.d: Dimensions are categorical fields that slice the view, and measures are numeric fields that are aggregated. Calculated fields add logic, and level of detail (LOD) expressions such as FIXED, INCLUDE and EXCLUDE compute aggregates at a different level from the view, for example each customer's first order date. Filters follow an order of operations: context filters apply before FIXED LODs, which apply before dimension filters. Extracts are fast snapshots, while live connections query the source directly. Parameters and actions make dashboards interactive.
concepts.e: {FIXED [Customer ID] : MIN([Order Date])} gives each customer's first order date regardless of the view, so you can build a cohort chart of customers by first-order month.
concepts.c: When would you use a FIXED LOD expression instead of a normal aggregate?
concepts.i: Expect LOD expressions, extracts versus live connections, filter order of operations, and how you'd build a dashboard.

concepts.title: Excel for analysts: pivots and lookups
concepts.kw: excel pivot table xlookup vlookup index match sumifs countifs conditional formatting power query formulas spreadsheet
concepts.s: Excel is still the most common analysis tool. Pivot tables, lookups and conditional sums cover most everyday analysis.
concepts.d: Pivot tables summarise data by dragging fields into rows, columns, values and filters, which is a quick group-by. XLOOKUP, or INDEX with MATCH in older versions, finds values from another table and is more reliable than VLOOKUP, which breaks when columns move and defaults to an approximate match. SUMIFS and COUNTIFS do conditional totals. Keep raw data in a proper table, separate from calculations, and avoid hard-coded numbers in formulas. Power Query cleans and combines files repeatably, and conditional formatting highlights exceptions.
concepts.e: =XLOOKUP(A2, Carriers[Code], Carriers[Name], "Unknown") returns each shipment's carrier name and shows "Unknown" for missing codes instead of #N/A.
concepts.c: Why is XLOOKUP safer than VLOOKUP with its default settings?
concepts.i: Analyst roles often test pivot tables, lookups and SUMIFS in a practical exercise.

concepts.title: pandas fundamentals
concepts.kw: pandas dataframe series read_csv loc iloc groupby agg merge join filter boolean indexing sort_values pivot_table python
concepts.s: pandas is Python's main library for tabular data. A DataFrame is a table of named columns, and most analysis is filtering, grouping, joining and reshaping it.
concepts.d: Read data with read_csv or read_parquet. Select columns by name, filter rows with boolean conditions, and use loc for label-based selection and iloc for position-based selection. groupby with agg is SQL's GROUP BY, merge is a join (with how='left' and friends), sort_values orders rows, and pivot_table reshapes long data into a wide table. Vectorised operations on whole columns are much faster than looping over rows with iterrows or apply. Watch for chained assignment warnings, and use .copy() when you mean to modify a slice.
concepts.c: Why is a vectorised column operation faster than a loop over rows?
concepts.i: Expect live coding with groupby, merge, filtering and pivoting, plus questions on loc versus iloc.

concepts.title: Data cleaning with pandas
concepts.kw: pandas cleaning missing values isna fillna dropna duplicates drop_duplicates astype to_datetime string methods str strip lower categories outliers
concepts.s: Real data arrives messy: missing values, duplicates, wrong types and inconsistent text. Cleaning it carefully, and documenting what you did, comes before any analysis.
concepts.d: Start by profiling: dtypes, isna().sum(), value_counts() and describe(). Convert types with astype, to_datetime and to_numeric with errors='coerce', which turns bad values into NaN so you can count them. Standardise text with str.strip(), str.lower() and mappings for known variants. Remove duplicates with drop_duplicates on the right key columns. Handle missing values deliberately: drop, fill with a sensible value, or flag them, depending on why they're missing. Check row counts before and after each step, and write cleaning as a reusable function.
concepts.e: df['city'] = df['city'].str.strip().str.title().replace({'Bangalore': 'Bengaluru'}) collapses ' bangalore', 'BANGALORE' and 'Bangalore' into one city value.
concepts.c: Why use to_numeric(errors='coerce') and then count the NaNs, instead of dropping bad rows straight away?
concepts.i: Expect a hands-on cleaning exercise and questions on missing values, duplicates and type conversion.

concepts.title: Exploratory data analysis
concepts.kw: exploratory data analysis eda profiling distributions histograms correlations missing values outliers univariate bivariate hypotheses
concepts.s: Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is the first look at a dataset: understanding its structure, quality and patterns before modelling or drawing conclusions.
concepts.d: Check the basics first: row counts, the grain (what one row means), data types, date ranges and key uniqueness. Profile missing values and duplicates. Look at each variable on its own with distributions and value counts (univariate), then at pairs (bivariate): metrics over time, by segment, and correlations between numeric columns. Look out for outliers, odd spikes, impossible values and tracking gaps. EDA should end with notes on data issues and questions or hypotheses to test, not just a pile of charts.
concepts.e: EDA on a returns dataset shows that 4% of rows have a return date before the order date, which is a data issue, and that returns spike for one apparel brand's sizes, which is a hypothesis worth testing.
concepts.c: Why is establishing the grain of a table one of the first steps in EDA?
concepts.i: Expect to describe how you'd explore an unfamiliar dataset, or to do it live in a take-home.

concepts.title: Notebook workflow and reproducibility
concepts.kw: jupyter notebooks reproducibility restart run all environment requirements version control parameters hidden state papermill
concepts.s: Notebooks are great for exploration, but hidden state and out-of-order cells make results hard to reproduce unless you follow a few habits.
concepts.d: Cells can run in any order, so a notebook can show results that a fresh run wouldn't produce. Restart the kernel and run all cells before sharing. Pin library versions in a requirements file or environment, keep raw data read-only, and use relative paths or parameters instead of hard-coded local paths. Put reusable logic in Python modules, keep notebooks for narrative and exploration, and clear large outputs before committing to Git. Tools like papermill run notebooks with parameters on a schedule, but production pipelines usually belong in proper code.
concepts.e: An analyst's churn notebook gave a different answer for a colleague because a filter cell had been run twice. Restart and run all, plus a pinned environment, fixed it.
concepts.c: What problem does "restart kernel and run all" catch?
concepts.i: Expect questions on how you keep analysis reproducible and when you'd move notebook code into a pipeline.

concepts.title: E-commerce data model: catalogue, carts and orders
concepts.kw: ecommerce data model catalogue product sku variant cart order order items payments shipments returns customers fact tables
concepts.s: An e-commerce data model links customers, the product catalogue, carts, orders, payments, shipments and returns, and getting the grain of each table right underpins every metric.
concepts.d: The catalogue has products and their variants or SKUs (size, colour), with categories and brands. A cart holds items before purchase. An order has a header (customer, time, totals) and order items, one row per SKU in the order, which is the grain for most sales analysis. Payments can be several per order (partial or retried), shipments can split an order, and returns usually apply to individual items. In a warehouse, typical facts are order items, payments, shipments and returns, with dimensions for customer, product, date and channel.
concepts.e: Order 5012 has three items, is paid in two attempts (one failed UPI, one card success), ships in two parcels, and one item is returned, so it appears in four fact tables at different grains.
concepts.c: Why is the order item, rather than the order, usually the grain for sales analysis?
concepts.i: Expect to sketch an e-commerce schema and explain the grain of each table and how you'd compute GMV and net revenue.

concepts.title: Clickstream and event tracking
concepts.kw: clickstream event tracking tracking plan page view add to cart events properties sessions sessionisation user id anonymous id segment ga4 snowplow
concepts.s: Clickstream data records what users do in the app or website as a stream of events, and a good tracking plan decides whether it can be trusted.
concepts.d: Each event has a name (product_viewed, added_to_cart), a timestamp, a user or anonymous id, a session id, and properties such as product id, price and screen. A tracking plan documents every event, its properties and when it fires, so teams don't invent inconsistent names. Sessionisation groups events into visits, usually ending after 30 minutes of inactivity. Identity stitching links anonymous browsing to the logged-in user. Watch for duplicate events, bots, client clock errors and ad blockers, and validate tracking in QA before releases.
concepts.e: After a release, added_to_cart fired twice per click on Android, doubling cart rates overnight. A tracking-plan check in QA would have caught it before launch.
concepts.c: Why do you need an anonymous id as well as a user id?
concepts.i: Expect to design events for a feature, explain sessionisation, and discuss how tracking errors affect metrics.

concepts.title: Marketing attribution
concepts.kw: marketing attribution last click first click linear time decay data driven multi touch channels utm incrementality marketing mix modelling
concepts.s: Attribution assigns credit for a conversion to the marketing touchpoints a customer saw, which drives where the marketing budget goes.
concepts.d: Rule-based models include last click (all credit to the final touch, the most common default), first click, linear (equal shares) and time decay (more credit to recent touches). Data-driven models estimate each channel's contribution statistically. All of them measure correlation, not causation: retargeting often looks great under last click because it targets people about to buy anyway. Incrementality tests, such as geo or holdout experiments, measure the real lift, and marketing mix modelling estimates channel effects from aggregate spend and sales over time. UTM parameters and click ids make tracking possible.
concepts.e: Under last click, branded search gets 40% of credit. A holdout test pausing branded ads in some cities shows most of those buyers arrive anyway through organic search, so its incremental effect is small.
concepts.c: Why does retargeting often look better under last-click attribution than it really is?
concepts.i: Senior marketing analytics interviews ask you to compare attribution models and explain how you'd measure true incrementality.

concepts.title: Pricing and promotions analytics
concepts.kw: pricing promotions discounts price elasticity coupons promo effectiveness baseline incrementality cannibalisation pull forward margin markdown
concepts.s: Pricing and promotions analytics measures how price changes and discounts affect demand, revenue and margin, beyond the headline sales lift.
concepts.d: Price elasticity is the percentage change in quantity for a 1% change in price; elastic products respond strongly. Promotion analysis compares sales with a baseline of what would have happened without it, from a control group or forecast, to get incremental units. Then subtract the costs: discount given away on sales that would have happened anyway, cannibalisation of other products, pull-forward of future purchases, and the effect on margin. Check whether promotions bring new customers who stay, or just deal-seekers. Markdown analysis decides when to discount ageing stock.
concepts.e: A 20% off coupon lifted shampoo sales 50%, but half the lift came from customers who'd have bought anyway and a rival brand's sales fell 15%, so the net margin effect was negative.
concepts.c: Why isn't the sales uplift during a promotion the same as its impact?
concepts.i: Expect to evaluate a promotion with numbers, explain elasticity, and design a test for a price change.

concepts.title: Returns analytics
concepts.kw: returns analytics return rate rto return to origin refunds reverse logistics reasons size fit damaged cod fraud apparel
concepts.s: Returns cost e-commerce companies heavily in refunds, reverse logistics and damaged stock. Returns analytics finds which products, customers and reasons drive them.
concepts.d: Define return rate carefully: by units or orders, by delivered or shipped, and over what window, since returns arrive weeks later. In India, RTO (return to origin, when a delivery is refused or fails, common with cash on delivery) is tracked separately from customer returns. Break returns down by reason code, category, brand, size, seller, pin code and payment method. Apparel returns are often size and fit problems, fixable with better size charts. Watch for serial returners and fraud, and calculate the full cost of each return, including two-way shipping.
concepts.e: Kurtas from one brand have a 34% return rate, mostly "too small". Comparing with its size chart shows it runs a size smaller than others, so the listing adds a "size up" note and returns drop to 21%.
concepts.c: Why should return rate be measured on delivered orders over a fixed window?
concepts.i: Expect to define return metrics, find drivers in a dataset, and estimate the cost of returns.

concepts.title: Marketplace seller analytics
concepts.kw: marketplace seller analytics seller performance cancellation rate fulfilment sla ratings gmv take rate commission onboarding seller churn
concepts.s: Marketplaces depend on sellers. Seller analytics tracks their performance, health and contribution so the platform can grow good sellers and fix or remove poor ones.
concepts.d: Key seller metrics: GMV and order volume, cancellation rate, shipping on time within the dispatch SLA, return rate, customer ratings and complaints, stock availability, and the platform's take rate (commission and fees as a share of GMV). Seller scorecards combine these, and tiers decide visibility in search and payout terms. Track seller onboarding (time to first sale) and seller churn. Compare sellers within the same category, since return and cancellation norms differ widely.
concepts.e: A seller scorecard flags 120 electronics sellers with cancellation rates above 5%. Lowering their search visibility until they improve cuts customer cancellations by a third.
concepts.c: Why should seller cancellation rates be compared within categories?
concepts.i: Expect to define seller health metrics, build a scorecard, and analyse marketplace supply.

concepts.title: Personalisation and product recommendations
concepts.kw: personalisation recommendations collaborative filtering content based frequently bought together cold start ranking ctr conversion a/b test
concepts.s: Personalisation shows each customer the products, offers and content most relevant to them, using their behaviour and similar customers' behaviour.
concepts.d: Simple approaches go a long way: best sellers by category and city, "frequently bought together" from co-purchase counts, and recently viewed items. Collaborative filtering recommends what similar users liked, while content-based methods use product attributes such as category, brand and price. The cold-start problem affects new users and new products, so fall back to popular or attribute-based items. Measure with online A/B tests on click-through, conversion and revenue per session, not just offline accuracy, and include diversity and business rules such as stock availability.
concepts.e: A "customers also bought" widget built from co-purchase counts raised add-to-cart from the product page by 6% in an A/B test, while a complex model tested offline gave only 1% more.
concepts.c: Why must recommendations be judged with an online A/B test rather than only offline accuracy?
concepts.i: Expect approaches to recommendations, the cold-start problem, and how you'd measure success.

concepts.title: Inventory availability and stock-outs
concepts.kw: inventory availability stock outs in stock rate out of stock lost sales fill rate dark stores quick commerce replenishment sku availability
concepts.s: Availability measures whether customers can buy what they want when they look for it. Stock-outs lose sales and push customers to competitors.
concepts.d: In-stock rate can be measured as the share of SKUs available, but a demand-weighted version, the share of product views or searches where the item was available, reflects customer experience better. Lost sales estimates what would have sold during stock-outs, using the normal sales rate. Track availability by SKU, store or dark store and time of day, because quick commerce stores can run out of milk by noon. Root causes include poor forecasts, late replenishment, supplier fill rate and wrong inventory records. Tie availability to the top-selling SKUs, where it matters most.
concepts.e: A dark store's SKU in-stock rate is 96%, but its demand-weighted availability is only 88% because the bestselling bread and milk run out every evening.
concepts.c: Why is demand-weighted availability better than counting in-stock SKUs?
concepts.i: Quick commerce and retail interviews ask how you'd measure availability, estimate lost sales and find root causes of stock-outs.

questions.q: Which chart would you use to show a trend, compare categories, show a distribution, and show a relationship?

p.t: Line chart for trends over time
Histogram or box plot for distributions
Avoid pie charts for many parts

questions.a: A line chart for trends over time, like daily orders. A bar chart, sorted, to compare categories such as revenue by city. A histogram or box plot to show a distribution, such as delivery times. A scatter plot for the relationship between two numeric variables, like discount and conversion. I'd avoid pie charts except for a few parts of one whole, because bars are easier to compare.

questions.q: How would you improve a dashboard chart that stakeholders find confusing?

p.t: Put the message in the title
Choose the right chart type and axis

questions.a: I'd put the main message in the title, such as "Android conversion fell after v6.2", rather than a label like "Conversion by platform". Remove clutter: heavy gridlines, 3D effects and unnecessary decimals. Use colour to highlight the one series that matters and grey for the rest. Label lines directly instead of relying on a legend. And check the chart type and axis fit the question, for example bars starting at zero.

questions.q: How would you present an analysis to a senior executive with five minutes?

p.t: Lead with the answer and recommendation
Two or three pieces of supporting evidence

questions.a: Lead with the answer and recommendation in the first sentence, then quantify the business impact, for example about Rs 40 lakh a quarter at stake. Back it with two or three pieces of supporting evidence, each on one clear chart. Be honest about confidence and caveats, such as what the data can't show. Finish with a clear ask: the decision I need from them and the next steps with owners. The method and detail go in an appendix.

questions.q: How do you tailor the same analysis for executives and for an analytics team?
questions.a: For executives I focus on the impact, the decision they face and my recommendation, in business terms. For an analytics team I go into the method, assumptions, data sources and limitations so they can challenge or reuse the work. The level of detail differs, with deeper material in an appendix, and I avoid jargon with non-technical audiences, using their language and metrics. But the core message stays the same and consistent for both.

questions.q: What's the difference between a measure and a calculated column in Power BI?

p.t: Calculated column computed per row at refresh

questions.a: A calculated column is computed row by row when the data refreshes and is stored in the model, which increases model size; it's useful for things like categorising rows to use in slicers. A measure is evaluated at query time in the current filter context, so it responds to slicers, filters and visuals. Aggregations such as total sales, margin percentage or year-on-year growth should be measures.

questions.q: What does CALCULATE do in DAX? Give an example.

p.t: Evaluates an expression in a modified filter context

questions.a: CALCULATE evaluates an expression in a modified filter context: it can add, remove or replace filters before computing. For example, Sales LY = CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date])) shows last year's sales for whatever period is selected, which needs a proper date table. And CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALL(Product)) ignores product filters, so dividing by it gives each product's share of total.

questions.q: Explain Tableau's FIXED, INCLUDE and EXCLUDE level of detail expressions.

p.t: FIXED computes at the specified dimensions regardless of the view
INCLUDE adds a finer level than the view
EXCLUDE removes a dimension from the view's level
Example such as first order date per customer

questions.a: FIXED computes an aggregate at the dimensions you specify, regardless of the view, for example {FIXED [Customer ID]: MIN([Order Date])} for each customer's first order date. INCLUDE adds a finer level than the view, such as average sales per customer shown by region. EXCLUDE removes a dimension from the view's level, for example to compare each month against the yearly total. Note that FIXED is calculated before dimension filters, so use a context filter if a filter should affect it.

questions.q: When would you use a Tableau extract versus a live connection?

p.t: Live depends on the source's speed
Choose by freshness and performance needs

questions.a: An extract is a fast, compressed snapshot stored by Tableau, which makes dashboards quick and reduces load on the source, but it's only as fresh as its last scheduled refresh. A live connection always shows current data, but performance depends on the source, so it suits a fast warehouse like Snowflake or BigQuery. I choose by the freshness and performance needs: extracts for daily reporting, live for near-real-time operational views.

questions.q: Why is XLOOKUP or INDEX/MATCH preferred over VLOOKUP?

p.t: VLOOKUP uses a column number that breaks when columns move
Can only look to the right
XLOOKUP has exact match and an if-not-found value

questions.a: VLOOKUP refers to a column number, so it silently returns the wrong column when columns are inserted or move. It defaults to an approximate match, which gives wrong results on unsorted data unless you set FALSE. And it can only look to the right of the key column. XLOOKUP and INDEX/MATCH reference the return column directly, can look left, and XLOOKUP defaults to exact match with an if-not-found value.

questions.q: How would you use a pivot table to analyse sales by region and month?

p.t: Show values as percentages or differences

questions.a: Start from a clean table with one row per order and proper headers. Insert a pivot table, put region in rows, order date in columns grouped by month, and sum of sales in values. Show values as % of row total or difference from the previous month to see trends. Add slicers or filters for category or channel, so stakeholders can explore it themselves.

questions.q: How do you do the equivalent of SQL GROUP BY and JOIN in pandas?
questions.a: GROUP BY is groupby followed by agg, for example df.groupby('city').agg(revenue=('amount','sum'), orders=('order_id','nunique')), using named aggregations for clear column names. A JOIN is merge: orders.merge(customers, on='customer_id', how='left'), where how sets the join type: left, inner, right or outer. I check row counts after merging, or pass validate='many_to_one', to catch duplicate keys multiplying rows.

questions.q: What's the difference between loc and iloc, and why avoid looping over rows?

p.t: iterrows and apply loop in Python

questions.a: loc selects by label, meaning index labels and column names, and accepts boolean conditions, like df.loc[df.amount > 500, 'city']. iloc selects by integer position, like df.iloc[0:5, 2]. Looping over rows with iterrows, or row-wise apply, runs slow Python code once per row, while vectorised operations on whole columns run in optimised C code and are often 100 times faster.

questions.q: How would you clean a messy CSV of orders in pandas?

p.t: Convert types with to_datetime and to_numeric

questions.a: First profile it: dtypes, isna().sum(), value_counts() and describe(). Then convert types with to_datetime for dates and to_numeric with errors='coerce' for amounts, counting the values that become NaN. Standardise text with str.strip() and lower(), plus a mapping for known variants such as city names. Remove duplicates with drop_duplicates on the order key. Handle missing values deliberately: drop, fill or flag depending on why they're missing, and compare row counts after each step.

questions.q: How do you decide how to handle missing values in a dataset?
questions.a: First understand why they're missing: a tracking bug, an optional field, or missing at random. Then measure how much is missing per column and segment. The options are to drop rows or columns, fill with a sensible value such as zero for no discount or the median, or flag them with an indicator column. Sometimes missing carries meaning, for example no delivery date means not delivered, which is a signal in itself. Whatever I choose, I document the decision.

questions.q: Walk me through how you'd explore a dataset you've never seen before.

p.t: Check quality: missing values, duplicates, ranges

questions.a: First the structure: what one row represents (the grain), row counts, data types, date ranges and whether keys are unique. Then quality: missing values, duplicates and impossible ranges like negative quantities. Next univariate: each column's distribution with histograms and value_counts. Then relationships: metrics over time, by segment, and correlations between numeric columns. I finish by writing down data issues and hypotheses to test, which is the real output of EDA.

questions.q: What red flags do you look for during EDA?

p.t: Sudden spikes or gaps over time

questions.a: Impossible values, like negative quantities or return dates before order dates. Sudden spikes or gaps over time, which often mean tracking or pipeline problems rather than real behaviour. Duplicated keys that should be unique. Suspicious default values such as 1900-01-01 dates, 0 or 'unknown' used as a placeholder. And totals that don't reconcile with known totals, such as monthly revenue reported by finance.

questions.q: How do you keep notebook analysis reproducible?

p.t: Restart and run all before sharing

questions.a: Restart the kernel and run all cells before sharing, so hidden state from out-of-order cells can't affect results. Pin the environment with a requirements file. Avoid hard-coded local paths; use relative paths or parameters. Move reusable logic into Python modules with functions, keeping the notebook for narrative. Keep it in Git with large outputs cleared.

questions.q: When should notebook code be turned into a production pipeline, and how?

p.t: When it runs regularly or others depend on it
Refactor into tested functions or modules

questions.a: When it runs regularly, or other people or dashboards depend on its output. Then refactor the logic into tested functions in a module, with unit tests on the key transformations. Add configuration instead of hard-coded values, and logging. Schedule it with an orchestrator such as Airflow, and add data checks and monitoring so failures are noticed. The notebook can stay for exploration and documentation.

questions.q: Sketch the core tables of an e-commerce data model and their grain.
questions.a: Customers, and products with their variants or SKUs, plus categories and brands. Orders hold the header, and order items have one row per SKU per order, which is the grain for sales analysis. Payments can be several per order, for example a failed UPI attempt then a card success. Shipments can split an order into several parcels. Returns are usually recorded at item level. In the warehouse these become fact tables around customer, product, date and channel dimensions.

questions.q: How do GMV, net revenue and AOV differ, and how would you compute them?

p.t: GMV is the gross value of orders
Net revenue subtracts cancellations, returns and discounts
AOV is revenue divided by orders

questions.a: GMV is the gross value of all orders placed at selling price, before cancellations and returns. Net revenue subtracts cancellations, returns and discounts, and for a marketplace it may only be the commission. AOV is revenue divided by orders, so it must say which revenue. Teams should agree a written definition for each. I'd compute them from the order-item grain, joined to cancellation and return facts, so the numbers reconcile.

questions.q: How would you design event tracking for a new wishlist feature?

p.t: Define events and when they fire

questions.a: Define the events and exactly when each fires: wishlist_added when the item is saved, wishlist_removed, and wishlist_viewed when the screen opens. Give them consistent properties: product_id, price, source screen and platform. Every event carries the user id, the anonymous id for logged-out users, and a session id. Document all of it in the tracking plan so names stay consistent, then validate it in QA before release by checking the events in a debug view.

questions.q: How do you sessionise clickstream events?

p.t: Order events per user by time
Inactivity gap starts a new session
Use LAG to compare with the previous event
Watch for clock errors and bots

questions.a: Order each user's events by time, then compare each event with the previous event using LAG. If the gap exceeds an inactivity threshold, usually 30 minutes, flag it as a new session. A running sum of those flags per user gives a session id. I'd use server timestamps where possible, since client clocks can be wrong, and filter out bots, which create very long or very fast sessions.

questions.q: Compare last-click and multi-touch attribution. What are their weaknesses?

p.t: Last click gives all credit to the final touch
It overvalues bottom-funnel channels like retargeting and branded search

questions.a: Last click gives all credit to the final touch, so it overvalues bottom-funnel channels like retargeting and branded search, which reach people already about to buy. Multi-touch models spread credit across touches, with linear, time decay or data-driven weights, which is fairer to awareness channels. But both measure correlation, not causation, and both suffer from tracking gaps across devices and lost cookies. So I'd validate them with incrementality tests.

questions.q: How would you measure whether a marketing channel is truly incremental?

p.t: Marketing mix modelling for the long term

questions.a: Run an experiment: a holdout where a random group of users doesn't see ads, or a geo experiment pausing the channel in some cities. Compare conversions in the treated and control groups to get incremental conversions, and from that the incremental CAC or ROAS, which is often much lower than attribution suggests. For long-term planning across channels, marketing mix modelling estimates effects from spend and sales over time. Then calibrate attribution models with the test results.

questions.q: How would you measure the true impact of a discount promotion?

p.t: Baseline or control for what would have happened
Subsidised sales that would have happened anyway

questions.a: Start with a baseline of what would have happened, from a control group of stores or users, or a forecast, and count only incremental units, not total sales. Then account for the discount given on sales that would have happened anyway, cannibalisation of other products, and pull-forward, where customers stock up and buy less later. Finally look at the margin effect and whether new customers acquired come back. Only then do you know if it paid off.

questions.q: What is price elasticity, and how would you estimate it?

p.t: Percentage change in quantity per 1% price change
Control for promotions, seasonality and competitors

questions.a: Price elasticity is the percentage change in quantity sold for a 1% change in price. Elastic products, above 1 in absolute value, respond strongly, while inelastic staples like milk barely change. The cleanest estimate comes from price experiments, testing different prices across stores or time. Otherwise, a log-log regression of quantity on price over history gives the elasticity as the coefficient, but you must control for promotions, seasonality and competitor prices.

questions.q: How would you define and analyse the return rate for a fashion marketplace?

p.t: Break down by reason, category, size and seller

questions.a: Define it as returned units over delivered units, within a fixed window such as 30 days, since returns arrive weeks after the order. Report it by units and orders, which differ when baskets are large. Keep RTO, return to origin from failed or refused deliveries, separate from customer returns. Then break it down by reason code, category, brand, size and seller to find drivers, such as one brand running small. Finally estimate the full cost per return, including two-way shipping and damaged stock.

questions.q: Returns rose from 18% to 23% this quarter. How do you find the cause?

p.t: Segment by reason, seller, brand and size
Look at customers and payment method
Link to changes like new sellers or policy

questions.a: First check the definition and timing: incomplete windows or a lag in return processing can distort a quarter. Then check for a mix shift, for example more apparel, which always has high returns, in the category mix. Within categories, segment by reason, seller, brand and size to see where returns rose. Look at customers and payment method: COD orders and serial returners often drive spikes. Finally link it to changes such as new sellers, a more generous return policy, or a change in size charts.

questions.q: What metrics would you include in a seller scorecard for a marketplace?

p.t: Sales volume such as GMV and orders

questions.a: Volume: GMV and orders. Reliability: cancellation rate and on-time dispatch within the SLA. Customer experience: return rate, ratings and complaints. Also stock availability for their listed items. Each metric is compared with sellers within the same category, since norms differ widely, and combined into a tier that affects search visibility and payout terms.

questions.q: Marketplace GMV is flat, but the number of active sellers grew 30%. What would you investigate?

p.t: Cannibalisation between sellers of the same products

questions.a: GMV per seller is falling, so growth is being diluted. I'd check how new sellers perform: time to first sale and how quickly they ramp up, since many may never sell. I'd look at concentration among top sellers and whether they lost share. On the demand side, check whether traffic and conversion grew, because more supply doesn't help if demand is flat. And check cannibalisation: new sellers listing the same products just split existing sales.

questions.q: How would you build product recommendations for an e-commerce site, starting simple?

p.t: Start with popularity and co-purchase rules

questions.a: Start simple: best sellers by category and city, plus frequently bought together from co-purchase counts, which often capture most of the value. Then collaborative filtering, recommending what similar users bought, and content-based methods using product attributes like category, brand and price. Handle the cold start for new users and new products by falling back to popularity and attributes. Measure everything with an A/B test on click-through, conversion and revenue per session.

questions.q: Your recommendation model looks great offline but didn't improve conversion in an A/B test. Why might that be?

p.t: Offline metrics don't match business outcomes
Recommending what users would buy anyway
Lack of diversity or popularity bias

questions.a: Offline accuracy often doesn't match business outcomes: the model may predict items users would buy anyway, which adds no incremental value. It may lack diversity because of popularity bias, showing the same best sellers everywhere. It might recommend out-of-stock or irrelevant items. And the problem could be the placement, slow latency on the page, or test issues such as a sample ratio mismatch, so I'd check the experiment itself too.

questions.q: How would you measure product availability for a quick commerce business?

p.t: By store and time of day

questions.a: The simple measure is the SKU in-stock rate, the share of SKUs available. Better is demand-weighted availability: the share of product views or searches where the item was in stock, which reflects what customers experience. Measure it by store and time of day, because dark stores run out of fast movers by evening. Estimate lost sales from the normal sales rate during stock-outs, and focus on the top-selling SKUs, where gaps hurt most.

questions.q: Stock-outs of bestsellers have risen in your dark stores. How do you find the root cause?
questions.a: I'd go along the supply chain. Forecast accuracy: did demand for these SKUs grow beyond the forecast? Replenishment: are orders placed late, or is frequency too low for their sales rate? Supplier fill rate: did suppliers deliver less than ordered? Inventory record accuracy: phantom stock, where the system shows units that aren't there, delays reorders. And store capacity limits and demand spikes from promotions or weather can empty shelves faster than planned.
